Pan de Muerto

Served at: Dia de los Muertos · Dia de los Angelitos

1 large loaf or 2 smaller loaves (Serves 8-10)Prep 45 min (plus 2-3 hours rising time)Cook 30-35 min

Pan de Muerto, or 'Bread of the Dead,' is a traditional sweet bread baked and consumed during Mexico's Dia de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) and Dia de los Angelitos (Day of the Little Angels) celebrations. It is a central element of the 'ofrenda' (altar) dedicated to deceased loved ones, symbolizing the cycle of life and death. The bread is often flavored with orange blossom or anise and decorated with 'bones' and a 'teardrop' or 'skull' shape on top.

Ingredients

  • 1/2 cup (120 ml) whole milk, warmed to 105-115°F (40-46°C)
  • 2 1/4 teaspoons (7 g) active dry yeast (1 packet)
  • 1/4 cup (50 g) granulated sugar, plus a pinch for yeast
  • 4 1/2 cups (540 g) all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting
  • 1 teaspoon (6 g) salt
  • 1 tablespoon (15 ml) orange zest (from 1 large orange)
  • 1 teaspoon (2 g) anise seeds, crushed (optional)
  • 3 large eggs, at room temperature
  • 1/2 cup (113 g) unsalted butter (1 stick), melted and cooled
  • For the topping:
  • 1/4 cup (56 g) unsalted butter, melted
  • 1/2 cup (100 g) granulated sugar

Method

  1. In a small bowl, combine the warm milk, yeast, and a pinch of sugar. Stir gently and let sit for 5-10 minutes until foamy, indicating the yeast is active.
  2. In a large mixing bowl, whisk together the flour, the remaining 1/4 cup (50 g) granulated sugar, salt, orange zest, and crushed anise seeds (if using).
  3. Create a well in the center of the dry ingredients. Pour in the yeast mixture, eggs, and melted butter. Mix with a wooden spoon or a stand mixer with a dough hook until a shaggy dough forms.
  4. Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 10-15 minutes by hand, or 8-10 minutes with a stand mixer, until the dough is smooth, elastic, and no longer sticky.
  5. Lightly grease a large bowl. Place the dough in the bowl, turning it once to coat. Cover the bowl with plastic wrap or a clean kitchen towel and let it rise in a warm place for 1.5 to 2 hours, or until doubled in size.
  6. Punch down the risen dough to release the air. Remove about 1/4 of the dough and set aside for decorations. Shape the remaining larger portion into a round loaf and place it on a parchment-lined baking sheet.
  7. Divide the reserved dough into 5 pieces. Roll 4 pieces into long ropes, about 10-12 inches (25-30 cm) long. Use your fingers to create indentations along the ropes to resemble bones. Shape the fifth piece into a small ball or teardrop shape.
  8. Arrange the 'bones' on top of the round loaf in a cross pattern. Place the small ball or teardrop in the center where the 'bones' intersect.
  9. Cover the shaped bread loosely with plastic wrap or a kitchen towel and let it rise again in a warm place for 30-45 minutes, or until visibly puffy.
  10. Preheat your oven to 350°F (175°C) during the second rise.
  11. Bake the Pan de Muerto for 30-35 minutes, or until golden brown and sounds hollow when tapped on the bottom. If the top browns too quickly, you can loosely tent it with aluminum foil.
  12. Remove the bread from the oven and let it cool on a wire rack for about 10-15 minutes.
  13. While still warm, brush the entire surface of the bread generously with the 1/4 cup (56 g) melted butter, then sprinkle or roll it in the 1/2 cup (100 g) granulated sugar until well coated.
  14. Serve warm or at room temperature. Pan de Muerto is best enjoyed fresh.

Tips

  • For a more pronounced orange flavor, you can add 1/2 teaspoon of orange blossom water to the dough along with the orange zest.
  • If you prefer not to use anise seeds, you can omit them or substitute with 1/2 teaspoon of anise extract.
  • Pan de Muerto is best consumed within 1-2 days. Store it in an airtight container at room temperature to keep it fresh.
